acquisition.why: Inbound channels work: SEO, Etsy and Google Shopping ads for custom gifts. Agents can run the listings and ads. Exact-match domain traffic as the source had isn't replicable cheaply [E].

onboarding.why: Customers upload photos and pick options through a web form. Proof approvals and revision requests still need checking.

delivery.why: This is physical manufacturing. Even with a print-on-demand or Asian factory partner, quality control, shipping and returns stay in the physical world.

support.why: Custom likeness complaints, damaged figures and delays mean frequent human judgement.

scores.R_why: Sourcing a reliable custom-sculpt supplier, sampling and stock handling don't fit £300 or 6-8 h/week. AI 3D-print figurine competitors exist [E]. Feasible only as Etsy dropship with an existing supplier.
scores.M_why: UK custom bobblehead and figurine sellers are established on Etsy and Amazon. Margins are squeezed by Chinese direct sellers [E].
scores.one_line: Physical custom manufacturing with hearsay, hypothetical revenue maths; a crowded gift niche with little to automate beyond the storefront.

acquisition.why: The cases that worked rely on in-person walk-ins, ringless voicemail and cold SMS to sole traders, which are PECR-restricted in the UK. Paid ads and inbound content are possible but expensive in a crowded niche [E]. Cold email only works for limited companies (dental practices, some trades).

onboarding.why: Template plus website or GBP scrape gets most of the setup done. Phone number forwarding and calendar connection need client coordination and a human check.

delivery.why: The AI agent answers calls unattended. Periodic transcript review and knowledge-base fixes are still needed.

support.why: Mis-bookings and wrong answers lead to angry owner calls. Small-business clients expect a human.

scores.R_why: The technology is easy, but sales are relationship and demo-driven, which clashes with 6-8 h/week and agent-only operation. UK trades are mostly sole traders, so cold outreach is not allowed. Liability for AI disclosure, call recording and GDPR sits with Ricardo.
scores.M_why: Saturated by 2026: GHL agencies everywhere, and native AI receptionists from Google, telcos and booking platforms (Fresha, Booksy) commoditise it [E].
scores.one_line: Well-evidenced (15 videos), but UK acquisition needs in-person or human sales and the product is commoditising fast. Poor fit for an approve-only agent business.

acquisition.why: Couple traffic can come from SEO and paid social, both inbound. Vendor-side sales need cold email, which is fine only for limited companies; many UK wedding vendors are sole traders, so they must come inbound.

delivery.why: Directory software and agent-maintained listings, with occasional data-accuracy checks.

support.why: Listing edits and removal requests are mostly routine. Disputes are rare.

scores.R_why: Cheap to build and fits Ricardo's skills and hours. The hard part is the slow SEO ramp and a vendor-monetisation chicken-and-egg problem. Scraped listings need a GDPR legitimate-interest assessment. A niche angle such as BYO-food venues or quirky vendors in London/Kent is realistic [E].
scores.M_why: Hitched, Bridebook and Guides for Brides dominate UK wedding search. AI search answers erode directory click-through [E]. Long-tail niches remain thin but small.
scores.one_line: Agent-friendly and cheap to start, but evidence is a hypothetical host musing and the incumbents plus AI search make monetisation slow.

acquisition.why: Runs through app stores, paid TikTok/Meta and UGC creators, all inbound. Agents can produce slideshow content, but creative testing and creator deals need oversight. Highly platform-dependent.

delivery.why: A vision model scores the photo and generates the plan unattended.

support.why: Refund requests and review handling are mostly templated. Policy flags from App Store review need human attention.

scores.R_why: Ricardo can build it. But growth needs ad spend far above £300, and the founder cites 5-10% margins. Body-image, ASA health-claim and app-store risks apply. The audience is 15-30, so age-gating and UK Online Safety/children's code issues arise [E].
scores.M_why: Looksmaxxing/body-rating apps are a crowded copycat wave by 2026. Ad costs are high and retention is weak per the speakers.
scores.one_line: Fully automatable product, but success hinges on paid-social and creator spend well beyond budget, in a saturated, policy-risky niche.

acquisition.why: SEO for free invoicing tools is possible but the space is crowded. Cold email works only for limited companies; most target tradespeople are sole traders, so cold outreach to them is banned.

onboarding.why: Self-serve signup plus Stripe Connect KYC.

billing.why: Revenue comes automatically as an application fee via Stripe Connect.

support.why: Payment disputes, failed payouts and VAT/MTD questions are money-related and need care.

scores.R_why: The build is easy, but a meaningful income needs high payment volume. UK interchange caps and Stripe Connect platform obligations apply. Free tiers from Xero, FreeAgent (via NatWest) and Zettle already exist [E].
scores.M_why: UK invoicing and payments are saturated with free bank-bundled tools. The payments markup is easily undercut.
scores.one_line: Elegant agent-run software, but untested by the speakers; UK free bank-bundled competitors and thin payment margins leave little room.

acquisition.why: Inbound channels: WordPress plugin directory, SEO, affiliate-marketer communities. The original success relied on a large existing list Ricardo lacks.

support.why: Integration and API issues (Amazon PA-API access rules) are mostly answerable by agents from docs.

scores.R_why: Buildable cheaply now, but the narrator's own data shows weak demand: $50k earned back on $120k over 3 years.
scores.M_why: Amazon affiliate sites are shrinking after Google updates and AI Overviews. Free plugins (AAWP, Lasso alternatives) already cover the need [E].
scores.one_line: Fully automatable, but an honest first-hand post-mortem shows weak demand in a declining affiliate-site market; avoid.

acquisition.why: Local Facebook/Meta ads and booking platforms like Playtomic are inbound and cheap per lead.

onboarding.why: Online booking and smart-lock access can be automated. Waivers are digital.

delivery.why: A physical venue: premises, cleaning, maintenance, insurance.

support.why: Facility issues, access failures and member disputes need a local human.

scores.R_why: Requires premises, buildout costing tens of thousands, planning/change of use and insurance in London. That is far beyond £300 and 6-8 h/week, and the source host had his own building.
scores.M_why: UK pickleball is growing and dedicated indoor venues are scarce [E], but councils and sports centres are adding courts.
scores.one_line: Physical capital-heavy venue with only lead-cost evidence and no paying members; incompatible with Ricardo's budget, time and agent-run aim.

acquisition.why: SEO 'X alternative' pages, comparison content and directories (G2, AppSumo) are inbound. BuiltWith-targeted cold email is fine for limited companies only; many UK landlords are individuals.

onboarding.why: Self-serve works, but data migration from incumbents usually needs help.

delivery.why: SaaS runs unattended, with bug fixing via coding agents and human review.

support.why: Mission-critical workflows (rent, property records) bring urgent tickets and trust demands.

scores.R_why: Suits a technical builder with AI coding tools, and £300 covers an MVP. Choosing a UK-specific underserved niche (e.g. small landlord compliance) is key. The support load could exceed his hours if mission-critical [E].
scores.M_why: Vibe-coding makes cheap clones abundant, so clones themselves commoditise. Headroom depends on niche choice, and UK-localised verticals have some room [E].
scores.one_line: A generic strategy, not a validated business: buildable by agents, but success depends entirely on niche selection and inbound distribution, with no first-hand evidence.
